lawyer:
Qumrul Haque Siddique with Md. Abul Kalam Patowary and SM Harmuz Ahmed, Advocates -----For the petitioner and Respondent Nos. 6-11. 
Khair Ezaz Masud with Md. Mominullah Patwary Advocates -----For the Respondent No. 5.
parties:
Jahangir Maji ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Khurshid Alam Sarkar J : By filing an application under Article 102 of the Constitution, the petitioner questioned the legality and propriety of the notice issued by the Officer-in-Charge of the office of the Collector (Deputy Commissioner), Chandpur (hereinafter referred to as respondent No.2) vide Memo No. 2-6/09-600/RM dated 2-9-2013 asking the petitioner and respondent Nos. 6-11 to appear before Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Chandpur (hereinafter referred to as respondent No.3) for attending the hearing of Mutation Appeal Case No. 32 of 2013, which was previously adjudicated upon by the same respondent No.3 on 13-8-2013.

2. Succinctly, the facts of the case, as stated in the writ petition, are that three groups of people, claiming themselves as the owners of the three different pieces of land, mutated their respective lands vide three Mutation cases namely, Mutation Case No. 4191 of 2011-2012 dated 15-3-2012, Mutation Case No. 5825 of 2011-2012 dated 11-6-2012 and Mutation Case no. 5824 of 2011-2012 dated 11-6-2012. While the writ petitioner's right, interest and claim, conjointly with that of respondent Nos. 8-10, lies in Mutation Case No. 5825 of 2011-2012, Mutation Case No. 5824 of 2011-2012 is with regard to the record of right of respondent Nos. 6 & 7 and Mutation Case No. 4191 deals with the record of right of respondent No.11. After coming to know about the above records of rights in the names of the above three sets of people, respondent No. 5 together with other two persons complained to the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Chandpur (hereinafter referred to as the A/C Land) on 17-1-2013 that the names of the petitioner and respondent nos. 6-11 (for ease of reference the petitioner and respondent nos. 6-11 hereinafter would be treated as one group and referred to as "the petitioners", given that their interest is same and they seek the same remedy) have been wrongly mutated and thus, prayed for reviewing the order passed by him in the aforesaid mutation cases. Pursuant to the said objection, the above three Mutation Cases were reheard upon being registered as Review Case No. 154 of 2012-2013 and by order dated 10-6- 2013 the A/C Land upon hearing both the sides cancelled the earlier mutations recorded in the names of the petitioners. The above U-turn stance of the A/C Land in disposing of the Review Case No. 154 of 2012-2013 prompted the petitioners to prefer an appeal before the appellate authority namely, Collector of Chandpur (respondent No.2) who allocated the same for disposal by respondent No. 3 who upon hearing both the parties allowed the appeal vide order dated 13-8- 2013. Against the said order dated 13-28-2013 respondent no.5 filed an application before respondent No.2 who asked respondent no. 3 to deal with the matter. Then, pursuant to an order passed by respondent No. 3 on 1-9-2013 the impugned order has been issued by the Officer-in- Charge of the office of respondent No. 2 and, hence, this Rule.

3. Respondent No.5 contested the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition contending, inter-alia, that the properties in question are owned and possessed by him and recording of the names of the petitioners thereon by the A/C Land was erroneous and, thus, respondent no.5 had to approach the A/C Land with supportive papers detailing the true position as to the title and possession of the lands and prayed to him for undertaking a review exercise of his own order in order to arrive at a correct decision in recording the names on the lands. The A/C Land having been briefed about the up-to-date position regarding the title and possession of the lands rightly cancelled the mutations of the petitioners in presence of both the sides. It is alleged that against the said review decision when the petitioners appealed before respondent No.3, the latter set aside the A/C Land's decision passed in the aforesaid Review Case by adopting fraudulent means and, under the circumstances, he had no other option but to approach respondent No. 2 with a prayer for investigation into the matter and, thereby, rehear the appeal in presence of both the sides. It is claimed by respondent No.5 that his approach before respondent No.2 is not made invoking the latter's jurisdiction of appeal or revision, rather it is an application for review of the order passed by respondent No.3.

4. Mr. Qumrul Haque Siddique, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, places the texts of the impugned notice line-by-line before the Court and submits that the same is full of ambiguity and, thus, an ordinary person, like the petitioner, would not be able to comprehend its contentions. In an endeavor to elaborate his submissions on this point, he pinpoints to the Cause Title of the impugned notice which contains the word 'appeal' as well as the word 'revision' in chorus and submits that if those words are taken in their true sense employing their literal meanings, then the impugned order is liable to be declared illegal on the face of it inasmuch as there is no provision anywhere in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (SAT Act) empowering respondent No.3 to rehear an appeal.

5. He then takes us through sections 147, 149 and 150 of the SAT Act, which provide provisions for appeal, revision and review respectively, and submits that once the provision of appeal is invoked before a higher authority by any party to a Mutation Case, then there shall not be any scope to review an order by any authority. He emphatically submits that the provision of review should be exercised by the original Revenue officer, namely, the A/C Land only given that, other than exercising this review power, he does not have any dominance to revise his own order or he cannot sit in the appellate capacity to rectify an erroneous order passed by him. He argues that it was definitely not the intention of the Legislature to bestow all the Revenue officers, ranking from the A/C Land to Members of the Board of Land Administration, with all three types of jurisdictions, namely appeal, revision and review.

6. He comments that the scheme of this particular piece of legislation is on the verge of being frustrated because of the abuse of the above provisions by the stakeholders. To elaborate this facet of the argument, he submits that if an unscrupulous citizen wants to exhaust all the tiers as laid down in all these provisions, there will be at least 9 phases in adjudication upon a single dispute and it may take decades altogether for resolution of a mutation claim. He proffers that it was not contemplated by the Legislature that at each higher-tier of appeal before the Deputy Collector, Divisional Commissioner and the Board of Land Administration, there will bean opportunity of filing review application inasmuch as on each occasion at the upper-tier the appellate authority shall have ample power to do what can be done in the review capacity, including delving deeper into the matter. He earnestly requests this Court to make appropriate observations by interpreting the relevant provisions of this piece of legislation in order to make this law workable without making any provision of this law nugatory.

7. He candidly maintains that apparently though the petitioner could have invoked the appellate forum before the Divisional Commissioner, however, since the petitioner believes that respondent no. 3 does not have any jurisdiction to review his own decision, his approaching before this forum is a correct step. In an endeavour to simplify this point, he submits that he has considered writ jurisdiction to be an efficacious forum given that the Divisional Commissioner is not competent to interpret the legal provisions relating to appeal, revision and review as set out in the SAT Act. He argues that the Divisional Commissioner would not have been in a position to undertake an examination as to whether review is exercisable only at the original forum by the A/C Land or the same is also available at the superior-level authority. By making the aforesaid submissions the learned Advocate for the petitioner prays for making the Rule absolute.

8. Per contra, Mr. Khair Ezaz Masud, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent no. 5, submits that until the provisions of sections 147, 149 and 150 of the SAT Act are declared ultra vires by this Court, it is to be taken that the law is valid and in operation and, thus, as long as they remain operative, the concerned functionaries of the State are bound to follow the course of the said provisions and, hence, there cannot be any question as to the legality of the step taken by respondent no. 3 in asking the petitioners for rehearing of the matter towards reviewing his own decision upon issuance of the impugned notice.

9. He then reads out the definition of 'Revenue Officer' as provided in section 2(24) of the SAT Act and submits that under section 150 of the SAT Act all the authorities, starting from the A/C Land to the Board of Land Administration, are empowered to have reviews of their own decision and, accordingly, the Assistant Commissioner (Land) Chandpur after passing the initial order was competent to have a review of his own decision and, thereafter, the Collector (respondent no. 2) is also empowered to have a review of his own decision and, subsequently, the Divisional Commissioner following passing of any order by respondent no. 2 or 3 would be in a position to have a review and then the Board of Land Administration would also be competent to have a review of a decision passed by itself.

10. He submits that when respondent no. 3 on 13-8-2013 passed an order in exercising his appellate jurisdiction, respondent No.5, having felt aggrieved with it, was competent to file a review petition before the same authority. Pursuant to the filing of the said application by respondent No.5, he continues, the impugned notice has been issued by the office of respondent No. 3 in accordance with the provisions of the SAT Act and, accordingly, no illegality has been committed by taking up the matter for rehearing it in review capacity of respondent No.3. By making the aforesaid submissions, the learned Advocate for respondent No. 5 prays for discharging the Rule.

11. We have heard the learned Advocates for both the sides, perused the writ petition and the affidavits-in-opposition together with the annexures appended thereto which have been considered by us very carefully.

12. The prime question that calls for determination by this Court is whether following pronouncement of an order by the appellate or revisional authority under the SAT Act, the same authority has any prerogative or legal sanction to review its own order and the next question that is to be examined and adjudicated upon by this Court is whether the petitioner ought to have challenged the impugned notice before the immediate superior authority namely, Divisional Commissioner, irrespective of whether the move is termed as appeal or revision. Thus, our overall task would be to undertake a scrutiny as to whether the impugned notice dated 2-9-2013 has been issued in accordance with law and by a lawful authority.

13. The factual events, which took place at first at the tier of A/C Land in allowing the three Mutation Cases and cancelling the same later on and also the subsequent events of preferring appeal before respondent no. 2 and its disposal by respondent no. 3, being the admitted facts, there is no contentious issue before us and, thus, there is no factual issue involved in this case to be adjudicated upon by this Court.

14. In order to embark upon the examination of both the questions, we may profitably look at the relevant provisions of State Acquisition & Tenancy Act, 1950 namely, sections 147, 149 and 150 one after another sequentially. Let us first take up the provisions of Appeal which run as follows:

"147. Appeals-Subject to any special provisions for appeal made in this Part or in any rules made under this Act, an appeal shall lie from every original or appellate order made under any of the provisions of this Part by a Revenue officer as follows, namely:

(a) to the collector, when the order is made by a Revenue-officer subordinate to the Collector;

(aa) to the Commissioner of the division, when the order is made by the Collector of a district within the division; and

(c) to the Board of Land Administration when the order is made by the Commissioner of a division.

15. From a plain reading of the provisions laid down in section 147 of the SAT Act, three important ingredients may be found namely, (i) which type of order is appealable, (ii) the name or designation of the authority whose order is to be appealed against and (iii) the appellation or rank of the authority to whom the appeal should be preferred.

16. The expression "an appeal shall lie from every original or appellate order" implies that there shall not be any appeal from any revisional or review order. In other words, no appeal lies against an order which has been passed in exercise of revisional jurisdiction or review jurisdiction. By employing the word "shall" in the aforesaid phraseology, the Legislature has sought to emphasise that against an original or appellate authority's order, an aggrieved party should opt for preferring an appeal before the next superior authority in order of hierarchy as laid down in (a) to (c) of section 147 of the SAT Act.

17. The second component of section 147 is that the order should be passed "by a Revenue officer" in order to qualify an order to be appealable or to come within the purview of appeal. Revenue officer has been defined in section 2(24) in the following terms "any officer whom the Government may appoint to discharge all or any of the functions of a Revenue-officer under this Act or any rules made thereunder". Since it is apparent that the Assistant Commissioner (Land) and all other upward-ranking authority, including the Members of the Board of Land Administration, have been appointed by the Government to perform some functions under the provisions of the SAT Act, they are to be regarded as 'Revenue Officer's .

18. And the third ingredient is that the appeal should be preferred to the immediate higher authority and, thus, an aggrieved party should not jump to the Divisional Commissioner against the order passed by the A/C Land bypassing the Deputy Commissioner (Collector) and so on.

19. Let us, now, take up the provisions of Revision, which is reproduced below:

"149. Revision-(1) Subject to any special provision for revision made in this Part, the Collector may of his own motion within one month of the date of any order passed under this part by a Revenue-officer subordinate to him or on application made in that behalf within one month of the date of such order, revise such order.

(la) The Commissioner of a division may, of his own motion, within three months of the date of any order passed under this Part by the Collector of a district within the division or on an application made in that behalf within three months of the date of such order, revise such order.

(3) The Board of Land Administration may, of its own motion, within six months of the date of any order passed under this Part by the Commissioner of a division or on an application made in that behalf within six months of the date of such order, revise such order.

(4) The Board of Land Administration may at any time order the correction of any entry in a record-of-rights maintained under this Part or in a settlement rent-roll prepared and finally published under this Part which, it is satisfied, has been made owing to a bona fide mistake:

Provided that an order shall not be revised under this section if an appeal has been preferred against such order:

Provided further that no order for correction shall be made under sub-section (4) until reasonable notice has been given to the parties concerned to appeal and be heard in the matter.

20. Apart from the provisions of time-limitations for revision, two main features appear from the plain reading of the above provisions. Firstly, the power of revision has been conferred on all the authorities except the original authority, namely, the A/C Land. In order to qualify as a revisable order, an order is required to be passed by an immediate subordinate Revenue Officer and the same should be revised by the one-tier higher authority. Secondly, there shall not be any revision of an order against which an appeal is pending.

21. Thus, it is our understanding on the provisions of this law that either appeal has to be preferred or, in the alternative, a revision may be filed. However, instead of preferring appeal if a revision is filed, no appeal shall lie against the revisional order, as has already been discussed and observed hereinbefore, but further revision may be filed before one-tier higher authority.

22. It is to be mentioned here that though all through the SAT Act the expression 'the Board of land Administration is contained as the highest authority for dealing with the mutation cases and some other land-related functions, however, at present there is no such authority with the above nomenclature. The Board of Land Administration was created by the Board of Land Administration Act, 1980 and, accordingly, there was an amendment in the SAT Act by the Ordinance XLI of 1982 to incorporate the words 'the Board of Land Administration in place of the 'Government' in the SAT Act. However, with the passage of the ভূমি আপীল বোর্ড আইন,১৯৮৯, the said 'Board of Land Administration Act, 1980 was repealed and under the ভূমি আপীল বোর্ড আইন,১৯৮৯, a new forum namely the 'Land Appeal Board' has been created which, having taken over the functions of the 'Land Administration Board' since the repealing of the said Land Administration Act, 1980, is functioning till date. It means that the expression 'the Board of Land Administration' used in the SAT Act is to mean, for the practical purpose, the Land Appeal Board, the expression used in the ভূমি আপীল বোর্ড আইন,১৯৮৯,

23. Now, comes the provisions of review which seems to be most relevant one for adjudication upon the case at hand. The said provisions are as under :

150. Review by Revenue-officer-(1) A Revenue-officer may, on application made in that behalf by any party interested or of his own motion review any order passed by himself or by any of his predecessors in office under this Part, and in so reviewing any order, may modify, reverse or confirm any such order:

Provided that-

(a) an application for review of an order shall not be entertained unless it is made within thirty days from the date of such order or, when such application is presented after the expiry of the said period of thirty days, unless the applicant satisfies the Revenue-officer that he had sufficient cause

for not making the application within the said period;

(b) an order shall not be reviewed if an appeal has been preferred against such order or an application for revision of such order has been made to the superior Revenue Authority; and

(c) an order shall not be modified or reversed on a review until reasonable notice has been given to the parties concerned to appeal and be heard in the matter.

(2) No appeal shall lie from an order rejecting an application for review or confirming on a review any previous order.

24. On top of the provisions of the time-limitation for review, there appear three important aspects of these provisions of law. Firstly, by using the heading of section 150 containing the following wordings "Review by Revenue Officer", the Legislature has attributed a distinctive feature to the echelon of a 'Revenue Officer' mentioned herein this section from that of the other Revenue Officer as defined in section 2(24) of the SAT Act in the backdrop of the fact that while the Legislature incorporated the provisions of appeal in section 147 of the SAT Act, the heading of the said section simply was decorated with the word "Appeal" and, thus, purposefully abstained from employing the words "Appeal by the Revenue Officer" and, similarly, in incorporating the provisions for review, the Legislature willfully ignored the employment of the words "Revision by the Revenue Officer". Thus, it is our view that by using the words "Review by the Revenue Officer", the Legislature has sought to mean that there would be a review of an order passed by the A/C Land himself and no other Revenue Officer shall have the jurisdiction to review his own order. Thus, the higher authorities to the A/C Land have been kept out of the review jurisdiction for the reason that they have been endowed with other two jurisdictions namely, appellate and revisional jurisdictions.

25. Secondly, the jurisdiction of the Revenue Officer for review has been made unavailable vide Proviso (b) of section 150 of the SAT Act if an appeal is preferred or a revision is filed. Since Appeal or revision is required to be preferred/filed before a superior authority, thus, under section 150 of the SAT Act, only the A/C Land has been meant to be the Revenue Officer empowering him to review his own order.

26. Thirdly, when an aggrieved party decides for review, be it with an expectation of rehearing of the case or for mere correction of clerical mistakes in the order passed by the A/C Land, instead of preferring an appeal, it is to be presumed that he would pursue his case invoking revisional jurisdiction to the immediate higher ranking authority under section 149 of the SAT Act.

27. Our above view gets buttressed up by the provisions of sub-section 2 of section 150 of the SAT Act. The said provisions prohibit preferring an appeal against the decision of the Revenue Officer, be it a rejection of a review application or allowing the review application by reversing any previous order. In interpreting the second part of section 150(2) of the Sat Act, we hold that there is a printing mistake as the word "confirming", which has been underlined by us herein above in quoting the said section, does not generate any meaning resulting in rendering the said second part redundant. Thus, the.word "confirming" should be read as "reversing" to attribute the viable meaning of the sentence, otherwise the second part of section 150(2) does not make any sense. If it is read as "confirming", it becomes a repetition of the first part; meaning rejection of review. The Legislature, thus, has not meant the word as "confirming" in enacting the said second part of section 150(2) of the SAT Act. It is the Constitutional duty of this Court to furnish the appropriate meaning of a provision of law when there appears any ambiguity.

28. In the case of Amir Khan vs Controller of Estate Duties 13 DLR (SC) 105 it was held that the Court can modify the language to give effect to the manifest and undoubted intention of the Legislature.

29. In the case of Principal Secretary vs Mahtabuddin 42 DLR (AD) 214, our Apex Court approved the substitution of the word "shall" in place of "may" done by the High Court Division in an effort to attach the true meaning of Para 1A of MLO 9.

30. There is a series of case laws of foreign jurisdiction maintaining the view that where any word of a provision of law appears to be expressly inconsistent with the entire sentence, the Court may substitute a proper word towards rescuing the provisions from being nugatory.

31. In the case of Attorney General vs Lockwood (1842) 9 M &W 378 it was held that where the language of a statute, in its ordinary meaning and grammatical construction, leads to a manifest contradiction of the apparent purpose of the enactment, or to some inconvenience or absurdity which can hardly have been intended, a construction may be put upon it which modifies the meaning of the words and even the structure of the sentence.

32. In the case of India vs Filip Tiago AIR 1990 SC 981 it was observed that modification of language may be done by departing from the rules of grammar, by giving an unusual meaning to particular words, or by rejecting them altogether, on the ground that the legislature could not possibly have intended what its words signify, and that the modifications made are mere corrections of careless language and really give the true meaning.

33. In the case of Tirath Singh vs Bachiltar Singh AIR 1955 SC 830 the Indian Supreme Court viewed that where the language of a statute, in its ordinary meaning and grammatical construction, leads to a manifest contradiction of the apparent purpose of the enactment, or to some inconvenience or absurdity or hardship or injustice, presumably not intended, a construction may be put upon it which modifies the meaning of the words and even the structure of the sentence.

34. In the case of Salmon vs Duncombe(1886) 11 App. Case 627 the Court of Appeal of England opined that where the main object and intention of a statute are clear, it must not be reduced to a nullity by the draftsman's unskillfulness or ignorance of law, except in a case of necessity, or the absolute intractability of the language used.

35. In the case of Carmas. Properties Ltd Connaught Fur Trimmings Ltd (1965) 1 WLR 892 Lord Reid has said that he prefers to see a mistake on the part of the draftsman in doing his revision rather than a deliberate attempt to introduce an irrational rule: the canons of construction are not so rigid as to prevent a realistic solution.

36. In the case of Clapham vs National Assistance Board (1961) 2 QB 77 the following phrase "in any proceedings on an application under the last foregoing sub-section" was substituted by the Court as "in any proceeding arising out of an application" with an observation that sometimes, where the sense of the statute demands it or where there has been an obvious mistake in drafting, a court will be prepared to substitute another word or phrase for that which actually appears in the text of the Act.

37. In the case of Southern Pacific Co. vs Jensen (1917), 244 US 205 at 221 Holmes J. (1841-1935) observed that-

I recognize without hesitation that judges do and must legislate, but they can do so only interstitially; they are confined from molar to molecular motions.

38. In performing the functions of legal interpretation, this Court is required to minutely read through the ambiguous provisions concurrently with the other provisions in the same chapter on top of grasping the scheme of the law and, then, give a word/phrase appropriate meaning with sound reasoning.

39. Sir Edward Coke (1552-1634), in his book A commentary upon Littleton (the first part of the institutes of the laws of England), 1628, 19th edn, 1832, 97b commented that-

Reason is the life of the law, nay the common law itself is nothing else but reason; which is to be understood of an artificial perfection of reason, gotten by long study,

observation, and experience, and not of every man's natural reason; for Nemo nasciturartifex.[Nobody is born an artificer.]

40. To furnish reasoning in support of modifying of the second part of the phrase of section 150(2) of the SAT Act, a best effort so far has been put by us in this case.

<u>41. At the same time, we were not oblivious of the dictum that Courts are not allowed to cause any change or amend any provision of law. Even replacement of a single word of a statute is beyond the power of the Courts, if it tantamount to legislate a law. In this case, no attempt to legislate a provision has been taken by us, instead a bonafide endeavour has been made towards making the statute meaningful by giving it a reasonable meaning.</u>

42. Lord Denning, in his book The changing law, 1953, p. 106 said-The judges are too often inclined to fold their hands and blame the legislature, when really they ought to set to work and give the words a reasonable meaning, even if this does involve a departure from the letter of them.

By so doing they are more likely to find the truth.

43. Lord Denning, in his another book The family story, 1981, p. 174 wrote-

My root belief is that the proper role of a judge is to do justice between the parties before him. If there is any rule of law which impairs the doing of justice, then it is the province of the judge to do all he legitimately can to avoid that rule - or even to change it of as to do justice in the instant case before him.

44. The crucial issue to be taken into consideration by the Judges in this kind of situation with great care is whether they are attaching a different meaning to the provisions in course of performing the functions of interpretation. Here, if we read the word as "confirming" In section 150(2) of the SAT Act, the provisions of section 147 of the SAT Act shall be inconsistent to the second part of the provisions of 150(2) of the SAT Act inasmuch as appeal will lie against an order reversing the previous order passed by the A/C Land in his review jurisdiction. Thus, by attributing the said meaning, we are not transgressing into the domain of the Legislature, rather we are performing our functions of interpreting the law which we are oath bound to do.

45. However, it shall remain open for the Legislature either to concede to the printing mistake as detected by us and thereby insert the word 'reversing' in place of 'confirming', or following pronouncement of this judgment the Legislature shall be at liberty to incorporate a new provision in an effort to make the second part of section 150(2) of the SAT Act a cohesive paragraph.

<u>46. From a combined reading of the above three provisions, namely sections 147, 149 & 150 of the SAT Act, it appears to us that though a party to a Mutation Case before the forum of Assistant Commissioner (Land) is allowed to take his matter upto the last forum of the Board of Land Administration by way of preferring appeals upon exhausting each of the tiers sequentially one after another as laid down in section 147 of the SAT Act, however, if any party ever chooses for a revision or review, no appeal shall lie against an order passed in revisional or review jurisdiction. Usually, as a common practice, an aggrieved party to the order of the A/C land, at first, files a review application before the same authority invoking the provisions of section 150 of the SAT Act and, thereafter, prefers an appeal before the Collector, but the said practice has been going on for years on fallacy, misreading, misconstruction and misconception of the provisions of sections 147, 149 and 150 of the SAT Act.</u>

47. We hold the above view for two reasons.

Firstly, since in any of these three provisions no restriction has been imposed or limitation has been drawn as to the grounds a litigant is required to take for approaching the same authority for review of his own decision or to the higher authority for preferring appeal or filing revision, it would be an absurd proposition for the Legislature to mean that from the stage of Assistant Commissioner (Land) upto the phase of the Board of Land Administration, a litigant would be allowed to pursue all factual and legal issues in all the tiers, irrespective of whether it is the original, appellate, revisional or review forum. Secondly, from the wordings employed in section 147 of the SAT Act that "appeal shall lie from every original or appellate authority ", and the language couched in section 150(2) of the SAT Act that "no appeal shall lie from an order rejecting an application for review or reversing (cone firming) on a review any previous order ", anyone with ordinary prudence would be of the view that an appeal cannot be preferred against a revisional or review order. By holding the above view, we are not saying that if a party does not prefer an appeal from the original order, an erroneous order will be perpetuating due to ignorance about selecting the appropriate route of law. If a party under a misconception of law starts with resorting to the provisions of review, he will not be deprived of taking his matter to the higher authority for further examination as he is well competent to file a revision application to the collector and, then, to the Divisional Commissioner if dissatisfied with the Collector's order and, finally, to the Board of Land Administration, which is akin to the route of appeal inasmuch as like the appellate jurisdiction of any Revenue officer under section 147 of the SAT Act, all types of legal and factual issues can be examined in the review and revisional jurisdiction under the relevant provisions of the SAT Act.

48. The apparent reason behind not making any provision putting restrictions on the power of revisional or review authority, as has been imposed in the authority of the civil revisional or review Courts, are that the general people are not acquainted with the technical and limitational factors attached to the legal parlance of appeal, revision and review and they should not suffer for failing to select the appropriate route of law. All that a layman understands is that when an authority rejects his case, he should be allowed to approach the higher authority. Our above view would not seem to be inconceivable if anyone seeks to be familiar with the background-history and the scheme of the SAT Act. In a nutshell, however, it can be said that the said law was enacted for the well being of the peasants who were being humiliated by the Zaminders for decades. Therefore, keeping this aspect in view, for the interest and benefit of the commoners the Legislature has kept open and flat provisions for all the jurisdictions namely, appeal, revision and review empowering all the said authorities to deal with every aspect of a mutation case, including legal and factual issues, ignoring the necessity of framing rules or setting up separate guidelines for three different fora so that they may be able to avail a next forum in the event of their dissatisfaction with the order of the original Revenue Officer. At the same time, the Legislature was also cautious to specify the two different routes, namely, the appellate route and the route of review, in order to save the simple-hearted citizenry of this part of the world from being unnecessarily harassed by encountering the situation of 'sort of double jeopardy' by the unscrupulous litigants and their cohorts.

49. It follows that a party to a Mutation Case would either opt for the route of appeal or, in the alternative,go for review and, then, invoking any of the said routes he would be allowed to take his matter up to the last authority namely, the Board of Land Administration whose order shall be final.

50. That being the position of the law, as held by us hereinbefore, now let us apply the same in the present case upon dissecting the events that took place from the stage of filing the three Mutation Cases in question before the A/C Land up to the stage of issuance of the impugned order.

51. It appears that the petitioners initiated the said Mutation cases and the same were allowed by the Revenue Officer, namely, A/C Land. Then respondent No. 5 being dissatisfied with the said orders approached the same authority and, according to our interpretation, the said approach was made under section 150 of the SAT Act and the same should be termed as a review application filed by respondent No.5. When the A/C Land reversed his previous order, there was no scope to prefer an appeal given that the A/C Land  said order was not an 'original' or 'appellate' order, under the provisions of section 147 of the SAT Act. However, the fact remains that the petitioners had moved before the Collector without definitely knowing the name of the forum to which they are approaching or the nature of his jurisdiction, in other words, it was not known to the petitioners as to whether the Collector would treat their application as an 'appeal' or as something else.

52. From our scrutiny, it reveals that usually all the Collector Offices of our country use a pamphlet-type notice containing both the words "appeal" with a slash "revision", which appears in the said notice as আপীল/রিভিশন Therefore, the said move by the petitioners before the Collector is to be treated as revision in the backdrop of the operation of the words "appeal shall lie from every original or appellate order ". There is nothing to be prejudiced by the petitioners for treating the said move as "revision" instead of an "appeal" inasmuch as the extent of the powers, of the concerned authority, sitting in both the capacity, namely appellate or revisional, are same in entertaining the said second-tier move by an aggrieved party. In other words, when a Collector is approached by an aggrieved party against an original order of the A/C Land, the move shall be termed as an appeal and if it is against the A/C Land's order of review, it shall be termed as a revision and the remedy that will be provided to the aggrieved party by the Collector shall be the same since no different modus operandi will be applied in presentation of the aggrieved party's case and in conducting the hearing and pronouncement of the orders, irrespective of terming the move by the aggrieved party as an appeal or revision.

53. Accordingly, we hold that the move by the petitioners before the Collector was in the form of revision which was allowed by the Collector. Against the said order respondent no. 5 had only one option open and available, which was to file a revision before the Divisional Commissioner in the backdrop of the mandatory provisions of section 147 of the SAT Act in the following phraseology "appeal shall lie from every original and appellate order" but, instead, he opted to approach the same authority who has not been vested with any power to reexamine a matter already disposed of by him. Thus, when the office of the Collector entertained the above move made by respondent no. 5, the former exceeded its jurisdiction and, thus, the actions of respondent Nos. 2 & 3 in issuance of the impugned notice were without lawful authority.

54. Now, we are required to deal with the issue as to whether the petitioner's move before this Court against the aforesaid unlawful actions of respondent nos. 2 & 3 was an appropriate one.

55. It has been revealed from our categorical discussions on sections 147, 149 and 150 of the SAT Act that for an aggrieved party of a Mutation Case from the jurisdiction of the A/C Land to the Board of Land Administration, the Legislature has provided two routes namely appellate route and other route.

<u>56. Whenever an aggrieved party to a Mutation Case prefers an appeal against the order passed by the A/C Land, the former is to be said to have opted for appellate route resorting to the provisions of section 147 of the SAT Act inasmuch as the order passed by the A/C Land is the original order and the next order/s, which may be passed by Collector and, then, Divisional Commissioner against the said original order, are the appellate order/s. And whenever the A/C Land is asked by an aggrieved party to a Mutation Case to reexamine his own order, the said move by the aggrieved party is to be seen as invocation of his right through the other routes, first approach of the said route is under the provisions of section 150 of the SAT Act and, then, next steps would fall under the provisions of section 149 of the SAT Act.</u>

57. In the case at hand, the aggrieved party to three Mutation Cases, being respondent No.5, instead of preferring an appeal against the original order, had chosen to invoke other route under section 150 of the SAT Act by asking the A/C Land to reexamine his own order. Accordingly, the next move to the Collector, which was taken by the aggrieved party being the present petitioners against the order passed by the Revenue Officer under section 150 of the SAT Act, is to be termed as an application for revision under section 149 of the SAT Act. When respondent No. 5 felt aggrieved with the order of the Collector his next appropriate forum was to seek revision of the Collector's order before the Divisional Commissioner. But instead, when respondent no. 5 opted to approach the Collector asking him to review his decision, pursuant to which the impugned order has been passed, he inducted the petitioners in a wrong forum before the Collector again. The petitioners, at this stage, rightly found that the move made by respondent no. 5 was wrong and, under the circumstances, the appropriate course of action for the petitioners could have been to file a revision before the Divisional Commissioner.

58. While failure of the present petitioners to invoke the appropriate forum before the Divisional Commissioner shall entail the maintainability issue of this case resulting in discharging the present Rule, however, given the fact that respondent nos. 2 & 3 exceeded its jurisdiction in issuance of the impugned order, there appears a bizarre situation for this Court, for, on the one hand, this Court may discharge this Rule on the issue of the maintainability for not invoking the forum of the Divisional Commissioner by the petitioners, on the other hand, respondent no. 5 had also committed the mistake of non-invocation of the forum of upper-tier before the Divisional Commissioner.

59. Both the sides are, thus; at fault in choosing the appropriate forum and it is apparent that it happened due to the absence of any Rule outlining the guidelines as to which order is appealable and which one is revisable. In view of the fact that the specification of the two routes of the Mutation Cases was not done previously by the Executives or was not available in any judge-made law, we hold that none of the parties are to be held liable for having failed to approach the right forum, rather due to the petitioner's present move, this Court had an occasion to lay down the appropriate guidelines. Given the above scenario of this case, the present Rule should be disposed of with the following directions upon the concerned authorities of the country.

(i) The Ministry of Land shall notify that jurisdiction of review under section 150 of the SAT Act is available only for the A/C Land against his own order and, thus, there shall not be any review by the other higher Revenue Officers. In other words; the Collectors (Deputy Commissioners) and Divisional Commissioners: shall not exercise review jurisdiction, for, if any error is committed by them, in that event, the parties to the case shall not be prejudiced as section 149 of the SAT Act, in addition to conferring a right to an aggrieved party to approach the one-tier higher authority, empowers the immediate higher authorities to suo muto take up any matter for rectifying the said error. However, the Board of Land Administration, being the final forum under the SAT Act, shall have power to review its own judgment and order.

(ii) The Ministry of Land shall notify all the Collectors (Deputy Commissioners) that whenever they are approached by a party to a Mutation Case against the original order of the A/C Land, they shall treat it as an appeal and if they receive an application against a review order of the A/C Land, they shall treat it as a revision.

(iii) The said Ministry, in the same manner, shall notify all the Divisional Commissioners as well as the Board of Land Administration that they shall entertain an application as appeal if the move before the Collector was made under section 147 of the SAT Act and if the matter arises out of a review order passed by the A/C Land exercising its jurisdiction under section 150 of the SAT Act, they shall treat the move, all through from the Collector to the Board of Land Administration, as a revision.

(iv) The Board of Land Administration, however, shall be competent to order the correction of any entry at any time in presence of all the claimants of the land, if it finds any bona fide mistake in a finally published record-of-rights or in a settlement rent-roll.

(v) The Ministry of Land is directed to consult with the Bangladesh Law Commission aiming at introducing necessary amendment to the SAT Act and, upon scanning through the various provisions of the said Act together with the provisions of the Land Reforms Ordinance, 1984 ভূমি সংস্কার বোর্ড আইন,১৯৮৯, and ভূমি আপীল বোর্ড আইন,১৯৮৯,  they should consider whether they would (a) reduce the existing options of preferring appeal and filing review & revision on a single matter and (b) whether they would substitute the words 'the Land Appeal Board' for the words 'the Board of Land Administration' and (c) whether they would do the required corrections of typing errors, such as the one which has surfaced in course of disposal of this case.

(vi) The Secretary of the Ministry of Land is further directed to file affidavit-in-compliance before this Court on or before 27-9-2015 confirming that all the revenue authorities of the country have duly been notified by issuing official notifications.

60. The office is directed to send a copy of this judgment to (i) the Secretary, Ministry of Land, (ii) the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs (iii) the Law Commission of Bangladesh and (iv) the Deputy Commissioner of Chandpur at once.

With the above observations and directions, the Rule is disposed of, however, without any order as to costs. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby vacated.

End.
